## How this directory works

A maker earns a listing the same way a product earns a record: its own published documentation — a datasheet, a manual, an official product page — has to support at least one product record in the database. There is no submission form and no paid placement. If a maker's wireless line cannot be verified from its own documents, it is not listed, however well known the brand is. That rule keeps the directory small, and it is deliberate: a directory of everyone is a directory of no one.

Each row shows the protocols that appear in the maker's recorded products, the product lines this site covers, and how many records stand behind the listing. A maker's own page collects those records in one table, notes the releases and announcements the news line has covered, and carries the claim entry described below.

## Listing status

Every listing starts as **listed**: recorded by the editors from public manufacturer documentation, not reviewed or endorsed by the maker, and not a recommendation. A maker can **claim** its listing to correct product lines and point the desk at current datasheets; a listing becomes **verified** when the maker has confirmed the entry's facts with us. Status is shown on every row because the difference between "we read their datasheet" and "they confirmed this entry" is information a specifier deserves to have.

## What the directory is not

It is not a ranking. Makers are ordered alphabetically, record counts reflect documentation coverage rather than market position, and a maker with three recorded products is not "better" than one with a single, exactly-right module. Compare within a protocol and a product class, read the records, and let the datasheets argue.
